plan.topic: 'Nature's Ozempic' oats and fibre: what fibre, protein and eating order actually do to your body's own GLP-1 hormone, why that is far smaller and shorter-lived than semaglutide or tirzepatide, and how to use fibre well if you're on a GLP-1 medicine
plan.angle:
Keep the brief's structure with these changes:
(1) Chapter 4: Shukla 2015 (adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin) is reported for glucose and insulin only, worded as 'one small pilot study linked eating vegetables and protein first with lower glucose and insulin rises after the meal'. Add no GLP-1 claim unless the separate 16-adult paper is fetched and cited on its own. Say that no semaglutide or tirzepatide trial tested eating order.
(2) Chapter 3: quote the FDA's 21 CFR 101.81 heart-disease model claim exactly ('may reduce the risk of heart disease', diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol, 3 g a day soluble fibre from whole oats). Make no weight-loss claim.
(3) Chapter 6: quote the advisory sentence in full: 'Smaller, more frequent meals and avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment can help alleviate symptoms.' Then give our own uncited tip: build fibre up gradually with fluids, unless you've been told to limit fluids.
(4) Thumbnail: 'OATS VS OZEMPIC?' or 'OATS = OZEMPIC?' with the subtext 'A SMALL NUDGE VS A MEDICINE', one calm labelled character holding a bowl, no body imagery.
(5) Use the Guardian line only if the article is fetched and credited. Otherwise cut it.
plan.working_title: Ozempic vs "Nature's Ozempic": Can Oats Boost GLP-1?
plan.why:
Rising search ahead of January. The title sits next to big Ozempic videos for suggested traffic, and the body rests on settled primary sources (a physiology review, label section 12.3, FDA 21 CFR 101.81), so it should pass the fact-check first time. | fact-check: The topic is sound. It's an evidence-led myth-buster that fits the natural-GLP-1 pillar, keeps the medicine and food clearly apart, and has low misinformation risk. Most of the brief's claims check out, but there are three things to fix before scripting and two to watch.

Verified while screening:
(a) Shukla et al., Diabetes Care 2015, 'Food Order Has a Significant Impact on Postprandial Glucose and Insulin Levels', is a pilot study in adults with overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes, all on metformin. It measured glucose and insulin at 0, 30, 60 and 120 min. It did NOT measure GLP-1, so chapter 4 must make no GLP-1 claim from this paper. The 16-adult paper that measured GLP-1 is a separate publication. Use it only with its own citation after a content-check fetch, or leave it out. Still to do: confirm n=11 against the full text.
(b) The 2025 joint advisory exists: Mozaffarian D et al., 'Nutritional Priorities to Support GLP-1 Therapy for Obesity: A Joint Advisory From the ACLM, ASN, OMA and TOS', Am J Lifestyle Med 2025 (also in AJCN and Obesity). Its exact sentence is: 'Smaller, more frequent meals and avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment can help alleviate symptoms.' It sits in the GI side-effect / nausea section. Quote the whole sentence at that scope. Don't cut it down to only the fibre clause, and don't turn it into 'avoid fibre on GLP-1'.

Must fix:
1) Chapter 3 wording. The FDA claim under 21 CFR 101.81 is a heart-disease risk claim: soluble fibre from whole oats, as part of a diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol, 'may reduce the risk of heart disease'. Calling it a 'claim about lowering cholesterol' makes it sound stronger than it is. Quote the model claim from the eCFR text, with the 3 g a day soluble fibre condition, and mention cholesterol only as how the claim is explained.
2) Thumbnail. Muted and on its own, 'OATS = OZEMPIC?' spreads the myth. Add labelled subtext that answers it: 'A SMALL NUDGE VS A MEDICINE'. Or use 'OATS VS OZEMPIC?'.
3) Guardian intro line. It's unverified. Fetch the article and credit it by name and date. If it can't be found, cut the line rather than describing the trend vaguely.

Carry forward:
- Half-life figures exactly as the labels print them (semaglutide PI 12.3, about 1 week; tirzepatide PI 12.3, about 5 days) and in the Holst review's own wording (under about 2 minutes).
- Chapter 2: no figures unless they come from a fetched paper, labelled with its population and size.
- The SURMOUNT-1 average with its full population and 'placebo plus counseling'.
- Never imply that fibre, oats or eating order replace or match the medicine.
- No 'oatzempic' recipe and no other 'nature's Ozempic' products (berberine, supplements).
- The kidney caveat on protein.
- The constipation line in label wording.

script.hook_pattern: Myth attack with the answer in sentence 1. The 'nature's Ozempic' claim gets answered straight away ('only briefly'). By about 13 s the half-life numbers back it up: under about two minutes for your own GLP-1, about a week for semaglutide, about five days for tirzepatide. One open-loop sentence then points to the fibre-timing sentence in the joint advisory, which pays off in the fibre chapter.

factcheck.summary:
The science holds up. I checked these against the sources:
- Holst 2007: native GLP-1 has a half-life under 2 minutes, is made by L-cells, is broken down by DPP-4 and cleared by the kidneys.
- Ozempic label: half-life about 1 week, 94% sequence homology, albumin binding and DPP-4 stabilisation. The FDALabel version is effective 1 Jun 2026 (Version 20).
- Mounjaro label: half-life about 5 days.
- 21 CFR 101.81: the model claim wording, 3 g a day of beta-glucan, and the benefit working through blood cholesterol.
- Shukla 2015: 11 adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin, the same meal one week apart, measuring glucose and insulin only.
- The joint advisory: the exact fibre-timing quote and the protein-priority sentence.
- STEP 1 and SURMOUNT-1: the numbers, populations and comparators.
- Tolhurst 2012: mouse and cell studies, via FFAR2.

The framing is careful: the mouse and cell evidence is labelled, the "may" is kept, and the advisory isn't over-read as a fibre ban. The safety lines, the kidney-disease caveat and the prescriber line are all present. The one problem that needs fixing is the dates on the Mounjaro sources. S3 and S10 carry Zepbound's dates (Revised 11/2026, DailyMed updated 16 Nov 2026). The Mounjaro label on FDALabel is effective 27 Aug 2026 (Version 40), which matches the known date, so 11/2026 is wrong for Mounjaro. Fix that, plus the minor wording points, and it can render.

issues.problem: This is the same Zepbound date applied to the wrong drug. I couldn't read a Mounjaro Medication Guide date of 11/2026 from the PDF, and the current Mounjaro SPL is effective 27 Aug 2026.
issues.fix: Replace with the Medication Guide's printed 'Revised:' date as read from the PDF, or if it can't be read, with the date from the SPL: "Medication Guide in Mounjaro SPL effective 27 Aug 2026 (FDALabel Version 40)". Never use 11/2026 unless the PDF shows it.

issues.claim: Rosa, 49, who has prediabetes ... whether a GLP-1 medicine is right for her
issues.problem: Prediabetes alone is not an approved use for semaglutide or tirzepatide. Weight-management use needs obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition. Viewers could take away that prediabetes by itself qualifies.
issues.fix: s10 narration: "Imagine Rosa, forty-nine, who has overweight and prediabetes. She watches that clip and wonders whether oats could do the job, so she could skip that conversation with her doctor."

issues.claim: eleven adults with overweight or obesity and type two diabetes, all taking metformin
issues.problem: Mostly accurate: the mean BMI was 32.9. The letter itself describes the participants as adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin, so 'with overweight or obesity' slightly goes beyond what it states.
issues.fix: "One small pilot study tested it in eleven adults with type two diabetes, all taking metformin, most of them with obesity." Or keep the line if the full text's 'overweight/obese' wording is confirmed.

issues.problem: The eCFR URL sends automated fetches to a bot-check page (unblock.federalregister.gov). It probably works in a browser, but a mirror I could reach confirms the text.
issues.fix: Keep the eCFR URL and add a backup: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/101.81

hold_reason:
Not rendered: Fact-checker verdict REVISE: The science holds up. I checked these against the sources:
- Holst 2007: native GLP-1 has a half-life under 2 minutes, is made by L-cells, is broken down by DPP-4 and cleared by the kidneys.
- Ozempic label: half-life about 1 week, 94% sequence homology, albumin binding and DPP-4 stabilisation. The FDALabel version is effective 1 Jun 2026 (Version 20).
- Mounjaro label: half-life about 5 days.
- 21 CFR 101.81: the model claim wording, 3 g a day of beta-glucan, and the benefit working through blood cholesterol.
- Shukla 2015: 11 adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin, the same meal one week apart, measuring glucose and insulin only.
- The joint advisory: the exact fibre-timing quote and the protein-priority sentence.
- STEP 1 and SURMOUNT-1: the numbers, populations and comparators.
- Tolhurst 2012: mouse and cell studies, via FFAR2.

The framing is careful: the mouse and cell evidence is labelled, the "may" is kept, and the advisory isn't over-read as a fibre ban. The safety lines, the kidney-disease caveat and the prescriber line are all present. The one problem that needs fixing is the dates on the Mounjaro sources. S3 and S10 carry Zepbound's dates (Revised 11/2026, DailyMed updated 16 Nov 2026). The Mounjaro label on FDALabel is effective 27 Aug 2026 (Version 40), which matches the known date, so 11/2026 is wrong for Mounjaro. Fix that, plus the minor wording points, and it can render.
